title: From spaghetti to hub: why an integration layer
objective: Learners see that point-to-point integrations grow with the square of the number of systems while a hub grows linearly, and that one API change breaks n-1 point-to-point integrations but only one hub adapter.

recommended.why: An animated network that grows year by year makes the spaghetti visible and lets the changed system and its broken links light up in place.

alternative.why: Watching the spaghetti grow versus reading the curve: which convinces a steering committee?

assumptions: Worst case: every system exchanges data with every other system; real estates connect fewer pairs, so the numbers are illustrative
The company starts with two systems in Year 1 and adds one system a year
A hub or event-driven layer counts one connection (adapter) per system; the hub itself is not counted as a system
The API change is Billing retiring its v1 API; each broken point-to-point link needs rework by the team on the other end
With Salesforce names, Salesforce clouds are counted as separate systems; in practice some share a platform and connect natively
units: integrations: count of point-to-point links or hub connections
time: one system added per year
checkDescription: For every year the number of links equals n(n-1)/2 (point-to-point) or n (hub), every link joins two real systems (or a system and the hub), and the API change impacts n-1 integrations point-to-point versus 1 with a hub.

learnerPrompts.predict: Before you play it: with 8 systems wired point-to-point, how many integrations do you think the company runs, and how many break when Billing changes its API?
learnerPrompts.explain: Switch to Integration hub. Why does the hub need more connections than point-to-point in Year 1, and from which year does it pay off?
